solution:
An absolute scale is linear and passes through absolute zero, so on each scale the reading is proportional to the thermodynamic temperature. Both thermometers are looking at the same triple point of water, which is assigned \(200\,\text{A}\) on one scale and \(350\,\text{B}\) on the other.

Hence, for a body at one common temperature,

\(\dfrac{T_A}{200} = \dfrac{T_B}{350}\)

\(T_A = \dfrac{200}{350}\,T_B = \dfrac{4}{7}\,T_B\)

At the triple point, the solid, liquid and vapour phases of water coexist in equilibrium. That state occurs at one unique pressure and one unique temperature, so it can be reproduced in any laboratory and always gives the same reading. That is what makes it a standard fixed point.

The melting point of ice and the boiling point of water are not unique in this way: each depends on the external pressure (the boiling point strongly so), and both are shifted by dissolved impurities. Two laboratories at different altitudes, or using slightly different water, would therefore assign the same numbers to genuinely different temperatures, so those points are not reproducible fixed points.

The other fixed point on the Kelvin absolute scale is absolute zero, \(0\,\text{K}\).

An absolute scale has its zero fixed by nature (the temperature of least possible molecular activity), so only one experimentally realised fixed point is needed to fix its unit — the triple point of water, assigned \(273.16\,\text{K}\). The Celsius scale, having no natural zero, needed two.

Other fixed point: absolute zero, \(0\,\text{K}\).

The two scales are tied together at different points. On the Kelvin scale the number \(273.16\,\text{K}\) is assigned to the TRIPLE POINT of water, whereas the zero of the Celsius scale is the ICE POINT — the melting point of ice at one atmosphere.

These are not the same state: the triple point lies \(0.01\,\text{K}\) above the ice point. So the ice point is at \(273.16 - 0.01 = 273.15\,\text{K}\), and it is that number which must be subtracted to convert a Kelvin reading into a Celsius one:

\(t_c = T - 273.15\)

Using \(273.16\) would place the Celsius zero at the triple point instead of the ice point, shifting every Celsius temperature by \(0.01\,^\circ\text{C}\).

On the Kelvin scale the triple point of water is \(273.16\,\text{K}\), where the unit interval (one kelvin) equals one Celsius degree.

A Fahrenheit degree is smaller: \(100\) Celsius degrees span \(180\) Fahrenheit degrees, so \(1\,^\circ\text{F}\) interval \(= \dfrac{5}{9}\) of a kelvin. An absolute scale built with that unit therefore counts \(\dfrac{9}{5}\) as many units for the same temperature above absolute zero.

\(T_F = \dfrac{9}{5} \times 273.16 = 491.69\)

Triple point \(= 491.69\) units on that absolute (Fahrenheit-sized) scale, i.e. \(491.69\,^\circ\text{R}\) (degrees Rankine).

For a constant-volume ideal gas thermometer the pressure is proportional to the absolute temperature, so

\(T = 273.16\,\text{K} \times \dfrac{P}{P_{\text{tr}}}\)

Thermometer \(A\):
\(T_A = 273.16\,\text{K} \times \dfrac{1.797 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}}{1.250 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}} = 392.69\,\text{K}\)

Thermometer \(B\):
\(T_B = 273.16\,\text{K} \times \dfrac{0.287 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}}{0.200 \times 10^{5}\,\text{Pa}} = 391.98\,\text{K}\)

Absolute temperature of the normal melting point of sulphur: \(392.69\,\text{K}\) by thermometer \(A\) and \(391.98\,\text{K}\) by thermometer \(B\).

The relation \(T = 273.16\,\text{K} \times P/P_{\text{tr}}\) assumes the working substance is an IDEAL gas. Oxygen and hydrogen are real gases; at the finite pressures used here their molecules have a small but non-zero size and exert intermolecular forces, so each departs from ideal-gas behaviour by a slightly different amount. That is why the two thermometers disagree by about \(0.7\,\text{K}\) even though neither is faulty.

The further procedure needed: repeat the measurement with successively smaller amounts of gas, so that the triple-point pressure \(P_{\text{tr}}\) is made lower and lower, and extrapolate the readings to the limit \(P_{\text{tr}} \to 0\). All real gases approach ideal behaviour as the pressure tends to zero, so in that limit the two thermometers converge to the same value — the true ideal-gas (absolute) temperature.

The tape is steel and is correct only at \(27.0\,^\circ\text{C}\). At \(45.0\,^\circ\text{C}\) the tape itself has expanded, so each of its printed centimetre divisions is longer than a true centimetre and the tape UNDER-reads.

Tape correction factor: \(1 + \alpha\,\Delta T = 1 + (1.20 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{K}^{-1})(45.0 - 27.0) = 1.000216\)

Actual length of the rod at \(45.0\,^\circ\text{C}\):
\(L = 63.0\,\text{cm} \times 1.000216 = 63.0136\,\text{cm}\)

At \(27.0\,^\circ\text{C}\) the rod (also steel) contracts by the same factor, and the tape is then correctly calibrated:
\(L' = \dfrac{63.0136\,\text{cm}}{1.000216} = 63.0\,\text{cm}\)

Actual length on the hot day \(= 63.0136\,\text{cm}\); length at \(27.0\,^\circ\text{C} = 63.0\,\text{cm}\).

The wheel slips on when the shaft has contracted until its diameter equals the diameter of the hole in the wheel, i.e. from \(8.70\,\text{cm}\) down to \(8.69\,\text{cm}\).

\(d_2 = d_1\,[1 + \alpha\,(T_2 - T_1)]\)

\(8.69\,\text{cm} = 8.70\,\text{cm}\,[1 + (1.20 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{K}^{-1})(T_2 - 27\,^\circ\text{C})]\)

\(T_2 - 27\,^\circ\text{C} = \dfrac{8.69/8.70 - 1}{1.20 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{K}^{-1}} = -95.8\,^\circ\text{C}\)

Dry ice sublimes at about \(-78\,^\circ\text{C}\), so this temperature is attainable.

The wheel slips on when the shaft is cooled to \(T_2 = -68.8\,^\circ\text{C}\) (about \(-69\,^\circ\text{C}\)).

A hole in a sheet expands exactly as a disc of the same material would: every linear dimension of the sheet, including the hole's diameter, scales by \(1 + \alpha\,\Delta T\).

\(\Delta T = 227\,^\circ\text{C} - 27.0\,^\circ\text{C} = 200\,^\circ\text{C}\)

\(\Delta d = d\,\alpha\,\Delta T = (4.24\,\text{cm})(1.70 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{K}^{-1})(200) \)

\(\Delta d = 1.44 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{cm}\)

The diameter increases by \(1.44 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{cm}\) (about \(0.0144\,\text{cm}\)).

The rigid supports prevent the wire from contracting, so the thermal contraction is exactly cancelled by an elastic extension of the same magnitude, and that elastic strain is what the tension provides.

Thermal strain that would have occurred:
\(\dfrac{\Delta L}{L} = \alpha\,\Delta T = (2.0 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{K}^{-1})(66\,\text{K}) = 1.32 \times 10^{-3}\)
where \(\Delta T = 27\,^\circ\text{C} - (-39\,^\circ\text{C}) = 66\,^\circ\text{C}\).

Cross-sectional area (radius \(= 1.0\,\text{mm} = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}\)):
\(A = \pi r^2 = \pi (1.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m})^2 = 3.14 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2\)

Tension:
\(F = Y A \alpha \Delta T = (0.91 \times 10^{11}\,\text{Pa})(3.14 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2)(1.32 \times 10^{-3})\)

Note that the length \(1.8\,\text{m}\) does not enter: the tension depends on the strain, not on the length.

Tension developed \(= 3.8 \times 10^{2}\,\text{N}\) (about \(377\,\text{N}\)), tensile.

The ends are free, so each rod expands independently and the changes simply add. \(\Delta T = 250\,^\circ\text{C} - 40.0\,^\circ\text{C} = 210\,^\circ\text{C}\), and each rod has \(L = 50\,\text{cm}\).

Brass: \(\Delta L_b = L\,\alpha_b\,\Delta T = (50\,\text{cm})(2.0 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{K}^{-1})(210) = 0.21\,\text{cm}\)

Steel: \(\Delta L_s = L\,\alpha_s\,\Delta T = (50\,\text{cm})(1.2 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{K}^{-1})(210) = 0.126\,\text{cm}\)

Change in length of the combined rod:
\(\Delta L = 0.21\,\text{cm} + 0.126\,\text{cm} = 0.34\,\text{cm}\)

Thermal stress arises only when expansion is prevented; here the ends are free, so each rod reaches its natural expanded length and neither is compressed or stretched by the other. The diameter \(3.0\,\text{mm}\) is not needed.

Change in length of the combined rod \(= 0.34\,\text{cm}\); no thermal stress is developed at the junction.

The mass is fixed, so \(\rho = m/V\) and a volume increase means a density decrease.

Fractional change in volume:
\(\dfrac{\Delta V}{V} = \alpha_V\,\Delta T = (49 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{K}^{-1})(30\,^\circ\text{C}) = 1.47 \times 10^{-2}\)

Since \(\rho V\) is constant, to first order
\(\dfrac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} = -\dfrac{\Delta V}{V}\)

\(\dfrac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} = -1.5 \times 10^{-2}\)

The density decreases by a fraction \(1.5 \times 10^{-2}\), i.e. by about \(1.5\%\).

Only half the power heats the block, and the time is \(2.5\ \text{min} = 150\,\text{s}\).

Heat delivered to the block:
\(Q = 0.50 \times (10 \times 10^{3}\,\text{W}) \times (150\,\text{s}) = 7.5 \times 10^{5}\,\text{J}\)

Convert the specific heat to SI: \(s = 0.91\,\text{J g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} = 910\,\text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\).

\(\Delta T = \dfrac{Q}{m s} = \dfrac{7.5 \times 10^{5}\,\text{J}}{(8.0\,\text{kg})(910\,\text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1})}\)

\(\Delta T = 103\,^\circ\text{C}\)

The maximum ice melts if all the heat given out by the copper as it cools to \(0\,^\circ\text{C}\) goes into melting ice.

Convert to SI: \(s_{\text{Cu}} = 0.39\,\text{J g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} = 390\,\text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\); \(L_f = 335\,\text{J g}^{-1} = 335 \times 10^{3}\,\text{J kg}^{-1}\).

Heat released by the copper block:
\(Q = m s \Delta T = (2.5\,\text{kg})(390\,\text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1})(500\,^\circ\text{C} - 0\,^\circ\text{C}) = 4.875 \times 10^{5}\,\text{J}\)

Mass of ice melted:
\(m_{\text{ice}} = \dfrac{Q}{L_f} = \dfrac{4.875 \times 10^{5}\,\text{J}}{335 \times 10^{3}\,\text{J kg}^{-1}}\)

\(m_{\text{ice}} = 1.5\,\text{kg}\) (about \(1.46\,\text{kg}\))

The water equivalent of the calorimeter is the mass of water that would absorb the same heat for the same rise, so water and calorimeter together behave as \(0.150\,\text{kg} + 0.025\,\text{kg} = 0.175\,\text{kg}\) of water. (\(150\,\text{cm}^3\) of water has mass \(0.150\,\text{kg}\).)

Heat gained by water and calorimeter:
\(Q = (0.175\,\text{kg})(4186\,\text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1})(40\,^\circ\text{C} - 27\,^\circ\text{C}) = 9523\,\text{J}\)

Heat lost by the metal block:
\(Q = m s (150\,^\circ\text{C} - 40\,^\circ\text{C}) = (0.20\,\text{kg})\,s\,(110\,^\circ\text{C})\)

Equating,
\(s = \dfrac{9523\,\text{J}}{(0.20\,\text{kg})(110\,\text{K})} = 4.3 \times 10^{2}\,\text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\)

If heat losses to the surroundings are NOT negligible, then part of the heat the metal gave out never reached the water and calorimeter. Our \(Q\) therefore under-counts the heat actually released by the metal, so the value computed for \(s\) is an under-estimate.

\(s = 4.3 \times 10^{2}\,\text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\) (i.e. \(0.43\,\text{J g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\)), and this answer is SMALLER than the actual specific heat of the metal.

The difference comes from the number of degrees of freedom, through the law of equipartition: each active degree of freedom contributes \(\tfrac{1}{2}R\) to the molar specific heat at constant volume.

A monatomic gas has only \(3\) translational degrees of freedom, so
\(C_v = \tfrac{3}{2}R = \tfrac{3}{2}(1.99\,\text{cal mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}) \approx 2.98\,\text{cal mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\),
which is the quoted \(2.92\,\text{cal mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\).

All the gases listed are DIATOMIC. A diatomic molecule can also rotate about the two axes perpendicular to the line joining the atoms, adding \(2\) rotational degrees of freedom, so
\(C_v = \tfrac{5}{2}R \approx 4.97\,\text{cal mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\),
which is exactly the range \(4.87\) to \(5.02\) observed. That is why they are markedly larger than the monatomic value.

Chlorine's value \(6.17\,\text{cal mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\) exceeds \(\tfrac{5}{2}R\). The extra contribution must come from VIBRATION of the two atoms along the bond. Chlorine atoms are heavy and the \(\text{Cl--Cl}\) bond is weak, so its vibrational quantum of energy is small enough to be appreciably excited already at room temperature; in the lighter molecules (hydrogen especially) the vibrational modes are effectively frozen out.

Inference for chlorine: at room temperature its molecules have vibrational degrees of freedom excited in addition to translation and rotation.

Fall in temperature: \(101\,^\circ\text{F} - 98\,^\circ\text{F} = 3\,^\circ\text{F}\). Converting the INTERVAL to Celsius,
\(\Delta T = 3 \times \dfrac{5}{9} = \dfrac{5}{3}\,^\circ\text{C} = 1.67\,^\circ\text{C}\)

The body's specific heat is taken as that of water, \(s = 1\,\text{cal g}^{-1}\,^\circ\text{C}^{-1} = 1000\,\text{cal kg}^{-1}\,^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\).

Heat lost by the child:
\(Q = m s \Delta T = (30\,\text{kg})(1000\,\text{cal kg}^{-1}\,^\circ\text{C}^{-1})\left(\dfrac{5}{3}\,^\circ\text{C}\right) = 5.0 \times 10^{4}\,\text{cal}\)

All of this is assumed lost by evaporation, with \(L = 580\,\text{cal g}^{-1}\):
\(m_{\text{evap}} = \dfrac{5.0 \times 10^{4}\,\text{cal}}{580\,\text{cal g}^{-1}} = 86.2\,\text{g}\)

Average rate over \(20\) minutes:
\(\dfrac{86.2\,\text{g}}{20\ \text{min}} = 4.3\,\text{g min}^{-1}\)

Average rate of extra evaporation \(= 4.3\,\text{g min}^{-1}\) (about \(7.2 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{g s}^{-1}\)).

Heat leaks in through all six faces of the cube.

Total area: \(A = 6\,l^2 = 6\,(0.30\,\text{m})^2 = 0.54\,\text{m}^2\)
Wall thickness: \(L = 5.0\,\text{cm} = 0.05\,\text{m}\)
Temperature difference: the ice holds the inside at \(0\,^\circ\text{C}\), so \(\Delta T = 45\,^\circ\text{C}\).

Rate of heat flow:
\(H = \dfrac{K A \Delta T}{L} = \dfrac{(0.01\,\text{J s}^{-1}\text{m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1})(0.54\,\text{m}^2)(45\,\text{K})}{0.05\,\text{m}} = 4.86\,\text{W}\)

Heat entering in \(6\,\text{h} = 2.16 \times 10^{4}\,\text{s}\):
\(Q = (4.86\,\text{W})(2.16 \times 10^{4}\,\text{s}) = 1.05 \times 10^{5}\,\text{J}\)

Ice melted:
\(m = \dfrac{Q}{L_f} = \dfrac{1.05 \times 10^{5}\,\text{J}}{335 \times 10^{3}\,\text{J kg}^{-1}} = 0.313\,\text{kg}\)

Ice remaining after \(6\,\text{h}\):
\(4.0\,\text{kg} - 0.313\,\text{kg} = 3.7\,\text{kg}\)

All the heat conducted through the base is used to boil water already at \(100\,^\circ\text{C}\).

Rate of boiling: \(6.0\,\text{kg/min} = 0.10\,\text{kg s}^{-1}\).

Rate of heat supply:
\(H = \dot{m}\,L_v = (0.10\,\text{kg s}^{-1})(2256 \times 10^{3}\,\text{J kg}^{-1}) = 2.256 \times 10^{5}\,\text{W}\)

Conduction through the base (\(A = 0.15\,\text{m}^2\), \(L = 1.0\,\text{cm} = 0.01\,\text{m}\)), with the inner surface at \(100\,^\circ\text{C}\) and the flame side at \(T\):

\(H = \dfrac{K A (T - 100\,^\circ\text{C})}{L}\)

\(T - 100\,^\circ\text{C} = \dfrac{H L}{K A} = \dfrac{(2.256 \times 10^{5}\,\text{W})(0.01\,\text{m})}{(109\,\text{J s}^{-1}\text{m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1})(0.15\,\text{m}^2)} = 138\,^\circ\text{C}\)

\(T = 238\,^\circ\text{C}\)

For an opaque body the incident radiation is either reflected or absorbed, so the reflectivity \(r\) and the absorptivity \(a\) satisfy \(a + r = 1\). A body with large reflectivity therefore has small absorptivity.

By Kirchhoff's law, at a given temperature and wavelength the emissivity of a body equals its absorptivity, \(e = a\). A poor absorber is thus a poor emitter.

Hence a body with large reflectivity absorbs little, so it also emits little — it is a poor emitter. (If this were not so, such a body placed in an enclosure at its own temperature would emit more than it absorbed and cool below its surroundings on its own, which is impossible.)

On a chilly day the brass tumbler and the wooden tray have been in the room long enough to reach the SAME temperature, both below body temperature. So the difference is not one of temperature but of how fast each conducts heat away from the hand.

Brass is a metal and has a high thermal conductivity (about \(109\,\text{J s}^{-1}\text{m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\)); wood is an insulator with a conductivity about a thousand times smaller (about \(0.12\,\text{J s}^{-1}\text{m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\)).

When you touch the brass, heat is drawn rapidly from your skin and conducted away into the bulk of the metal, so the skin temperature drops quickly and the nerve endings register 'cold'. Touching wood, the little heat drawn cannot travel away, so the surface layer in contact with the finger warms almost to skin temperature and the tray feels much less cold.

What you sense is the RATE of heat loss from the skin, not the temperature of the object.

An optical pyrometer infers temperature from the intensity of the radiation reaching it, on the assumption that the source radiates as a perfect black body.

In the open, the iron piece is not a black body: its emissivity \(e\) is less than \(1\), so at temperature \(T\) it emits only \(e\,\sigma T^4\) per unit area instead of \(\sigma T^4\), and the surroundings are cold so there is negligible radiation falling on it to be reflected towards the instrument. The pyrometer receives less radiation than a black body at \(T\) would send, and therefore reports a temperature lower than the true one.

Inside a furnace the piece is enclosed by walls at the SAME temperature. It emits \(e\,\sigma T^4\) and, in addition, reflects a fraction \((1 - e)\) of the radiation \(\sigma T^4\) arriving from the walls. The total leaving its surface is \(e\,\sigma T^4 + (1 - e)\,\sigma T^4 = \sigma T^4\) — exactly black-body radiation at \(T\). The instrument therefore reads correctly.

In short, a body inside an isothermal enclosure radiates as a black body whatever its own emissivity; in the open it does not.

The atmosphere acts as a one-way blanket for radiation.

Sunlight arrives mainly as short-wavelength (visible) radiation, to which the atmosphere is largely transparent, so it reaches and warms the ground. The warm earth re-radiates, but at its far lower temperature the emission is long-wavelength INFRARED (by Wien's law, \(\lambda_m T = \) constant). Atmospheric gases — chiefly carbon dioxide and water vapour — absorb strongly in the infrared and re-emit, sending a large part of that energy back down to the surface.

This trapping (the greenhouse effect) keeps the surface substantially warmer than the balance of incoming and outgoing radiation alone would allow. Without an atmosphere there would be nothing to absorb the outgoing infrared, so all of it would escape directly into space and the mean surface temperature would fall far below freezing — inhospitably cold.

Compare the heat that one kilogram of circulating fluid can deliver to a room.

Hot water entering at \(100\,^\circ\text{C}\) and leaving at, say, \(T\) gives up only its sensible heat, \(m\,s_w\,(100\,^\circ\text{C} - T)\), which for a drop of a few tens of degrees is of order \(10^{5}\,\text{J}\) per kilogram.

Steam at \(100\,^\circ\text{C}\) first CONDENSES in the radiator, releasing its latent heat of vaporisation \(L_v = 22.6 \times 10^{5}\,\text{J kg}^{-1}\) at constant temperature, and the resulting water can then cool further and give up sensible heat as well.

So each kilogram of steam delivers roughly an order of magnitude more heat than a kilogram of hot water at the same temperature. Less fluid needs to be circulated for the same heating, and the radiator stays at the steady \(100\,^\circ\text{C}\) of the condensing steam rather than cooling along its length — which is why steam heating systems are more efficient in warming a building.

Use Newton's law of cooling in the chapter's approximate form (Eq. 10.21): the rate of fall of temperature is proportional to the excess of the AVERAGE temperature of the body over the surroundings.

\(\dfrac{\text{Change in temperature}}{\text{Time}} = K\,\Delta T\)

First cooling, \(80\,^\circ\text{C}\) to \(50\,^\circ\text{C}\) in \(5\) minutes. Average temperature \(= 65\,^\circ\text{C}\), which is \(45\,^\circ\text{C}\) above the surroundings:

\(\dfrac{30\,^\circ\text{C}}{5\ \text{min}} = K\,(45\,^\circ\text{C})\)

Second cooling, \(60\,^\circ\text{C}\) to \(30\,^\circ\text{C}\). Average temperature \(= 45\,^\circ\text{C}\), which is \(25\,^\circ\text{C}\) above the surroundings:

\(\dfrac{30\,^\circ\text{C}}{t} = K\,(25\,^\circ\text{C})\)

Dividing the first equation by the second:

\(\dfrac{30/5}{30/t} = \dfrac{45}{25}\), so \(\dfrac{t}{5} = \dfrac{45}{25}\)

\(t = 9\ \text{minutes}\)
